Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On October 19, 2023, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) published its notice of a proposed rule to establish an Emissions Reduction and Reclamation Program. [1, 3, 5] The program, proposed under the American Innovation and Manufacturing (AIM) Act, is designed to manage certain hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) and their substitutes to minimize their release and maximize their reclamation. [1, 9] Key elements of the proposal included requirements for leak repair, the use of automatic leak detection systems, and the use of reclaimed HFCs in certain equipment. [3] The proposed rule was signed by the EPA Administrator on October 5, 2023, before being officially published in the Federal Register for public comment. [3] <2> In a report published on October 10, 2023, NOAA confirmed that September 2023 was the seventh-warmest September in the 129-year climate record for the contiguous U.S. The analysis for the month ending September 30, 2023, showed an average temperature of 67.8 degrees F, which is 2.9 degrees above the 20th-century average. The report also noted that New Mexico and Texas each experienced their warmest Septembers on record. <3> In a report from late September and early October 2023, NASA and the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) confirmed that the Arctic sea ice reached its sixth-lowest annual minimum extent on record, while Antarctic sea ice set a new record for its lowest maximum extent. The Arctic's minimum extent was recorded on September 19, 2023. [4, 5, 11, 13] Simultaneously, the Antarctic reached its lowest-ever recorded maximum sea ice extent on September 10, 2023. [2, 3, 9] These events are part of a persistent downward trend in sea ice, which scientists attribute to global warming and its feedback loops, such as the ice-albedo effect. [11] <4> A bipartisan coalition of 25 governors, part of the U.S. Climate Alliance, has announced significant new commitments to decarbonize buildings across the United States. [1] This initiative, announced on September 21, 2023, during Climate Week NYC, includes the goal of quadrupling the number of heat pump installations by 2030, aiming for a total of 20 million. [1, 2, 4] A key component of this commitment is a focus on equity, with the objective of directing at least 40 percent of the benefits to disadvantaged communities. [1, 3] The announcement featured several governors, including the co-chairs of the Alliance, and the White House National Climate Advisor, highlighting broad support for the initiative. [1] This effort is part of a larger strategy to achieve zero-emission new construction and accelerate the reduction of emissions from existing buildings, in line with the Paris Agreement targets. [1, 5] Several major heat pump manufacturers have expressed their support for this goal. [4] <5> The Biden-Harris Administration officially announced the launch of the American Climate Corps on September 20, 2023. This workforce training and service initiative aims to mobilize over 20,000 young people to work in the clean energy, conservation, and climate resilience sectors. The program is designed to create pathways to well-paying jobs and focuses on advancing environmental justice by including disadvantaged communities that are disproportionately affected by pollution and climate change. The initiative is a collaborative effort involving several federal agencies, including the Departments of Labor, Interior, Agriculture, Energy, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Following the launch, the administration announced further steps, such as interagency agreements and listening sessions, to establish the first cohort of members by the summer of 2024. <6> The U.S. Treasury Department released a set of voluntary principles on September 19, 2023, to guide private sector financial institutions in their net-zero financing and investment commitments. [1, 5] Announced by Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen, the 'Principles for Net-Zero Financing & Investment' are designed to encourage best practices and promote consistency and credibility for financial firms that have pledged to achieve net-zero emissions. [1, 2] The principles recommend that these commitments align with the goal of limiting the global average temperature increase to 1.5 degrees Celsius and are supported by a clear transition plan with measurable targets and metrics. [2, 4] The guidance focuses on Scope 3 financed and facilitated greenhouse gas emissions, which constitute the majority of a financial institution's carbon footprint. [5, 6] Alongside the principles, it was announced that several philanthropic organizations committed $340 million to support the development of research, data, and technical resources to aid financial institutions in executing their net-zero goals. [3, 8] <7> On Sunday, September 17, 2023, tens of thousands of protesters participated in the 'March to End Fossil Fuels' in New York City, marking the start of Climate Week ahead of the UN General Assembly. Organizers estimated the crowd size to be between 50,000 and 75,000 people. Participants marched with signs stating "Fossil fuels are killing us," demanding that leaders, including President Biden, declare a climate emergency and stop approving new oil and gas projects. The event featured prominent figures such as Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and actors Susan Sarandon, Ethan Hawke, Edward Norton, Kyra Sedgwick, and Kevin Bacon. <8> On August 25, 2023, a coalition of environmental and Gulf community groups, including Healthy Gulf, Bayou City Waterkeeper, Friends of the Earth, Center for Biological Diversity, Natural Resources Defense Council, and Sierra Club, filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. [1, 2, 8] This month was 0.24°C (0.43°F) warmer than any previous July in NASA's records, and the top five hottest Julys since 1880 have all occurred in the past five years. [3, 4, 7] Several individual states, including Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, and Wisconsin, recorded their warmest February ever. [3, 10] This warm month concluded the warmest meteorological winter (December 2023–February 2024) on record for the contiguous U.S. [3, 7] On a broader scale, North America as a whole also registered its warmest winter on record. [5, 6] <2> On February 29, 2024, NOAA's Climate Prediction Center (CPC) issued its climate outlook for March 2024. The forecast indicated a high probability of above-average temperatures for a significant portion of the central and eastern United States. Conversely, below-average temperatures were favored for California and other parts of the Southwest. <3> According to a report by NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) released on February 8, 2024, January 2024 ranked as the 10th-wettest January in the nation's 130-year climate record. The contiguous U.S. experienced an average precipitation of 3.18 inches, which is 0.87 inches above the average. Additionally, a significant arctic air mass moved across a large portion of the country from January 14-18. This event brought record-breaking cold temperatures, with some areas in the northern and central Plains experiencing temperatures 20 to 35°F below normal. Across the nation, from the Northwest to the Lower Mississippi Valley, this cold snap resulted in nearly 2,500 new daily minimum temperature records being set in 1,125 counties. <4> A widespread and intense storm complex impacted the southern, eastern, and southwestern United States between March 1 and March 4, 2023. This severe weather event produced at least 35 tornadoes, strong straight-line winds, and significant rainfall, affecting states including Texas, Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee, Kentucky, Indiana, and Ohio. The event was responsible for 13 fatalities and numerous injuries. With total damages estimated at $6.0 billion, it was the second-costliest weather and climate disaster in the U.S. for 2023, surpassed only by the Southern/Midwestern drought and heatwave. <5> In 2023, the U.S. faced a historic year for weather and climate disasters, setting a new record with 28 individual events that each caused at least one billion dollars in damages. This figure surpasses the previous record of 22 such events, which occurred in 2020. The total cost of these disasters exceeded $92.9 billion, a figure that may increase once the costs from a December East Coast storm and flooding event are fully tallied. The disasters resulted in a minimum of 492 fatalities. The 28 events were varied and widespread, including 17 severe weather and hail events, four flooding events, two tornado outbreaks, two tropical cyclones, one drought and heat wave, one wildfire event, and one winter storm/cold wave. <6> At the COP28 climate conference in Dubai, U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris announced a pledge of $3 billion to the Green Climate Fund (GCF) for its second replenishment period (2024-2027). This funding is intended to assist developing countries in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and adapting to the impacts of climate change. The pledge, which requires approval from a divided U.S. Congress, was part of a broader fundraising effort that brought the total contributions for the GCF's second replenishment to a record $12.8 billion from 31 countries. Other nations announcing pledges at the summit included Australia, Estonia, Italy, Portugal, and Switzerland. The announcement was met with mixed reactions, with some observers noting it matches a 2014 pledge by the Obama administration and highlighting the need for congressional action to deliver the funds. <7> The U.S. Climate Alliance, a bipartisan coalition of 25 governors, released its 2023 annual report titled, "All Hands on Deck: Securing America's Net-Zero Future with State-Led, High-Impact Action." The report, announced at the COP28 climate summit in Dubai, confirms that the member states and territories are projected to collectively reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 26% below 2005 levels by 2025, meeting their near-term goal. It details new state-level policies, programs, and investments from 2023 aimed at advancing climate action. The report incorporates analysis from Energy and Environmental Economics (E3), which used its PATHWAYS model to map various GHG emission scenarios through 2050, considering the impact of current and proposed state and federal actions, including the Inflation Reduction Act. <8> A Montana District Court denied the state's motion to stay the landmark August 2023 judgment in the youth-led constitutional climate case, Held v. Montana. The denial of the stay occurred on November 21, 2023, and was issued by Lewis and Clark District Court Judge Kathy Seeley. The original ruling found that a provision in the Montana Environmental Policy Act, which prevented the state from considering greenhouse gas emissions and climate change impacts during environmental reviews, was unconstitutional. Judge Seeley reasoned that she could not grant the stay because the case had already been appealed to the Montana Supreme Court, and further noted that the state failed to prove that it would suffer irreparable harm by analyzing climate impacts. Subsequently, the Montana Supreme Court also denied the state's request for a stay on January 16, 2024, finding no good cause to pause the lower court's ruling pending the full appeal.

Notably, on April 27, a violent, low-end EF-4 tornado struck Marietta, Oklahoma, leading to one death and significant destruction, including a large warehouse and a grocery store. This funding is part of a larger, coordinated North American strategy, involving policy alignment and bilateral alliances with Canada, to aggressively build and support domestic supply chains for the clean energy sector. <2> In the first eight months of 2025, from January through August, the United States added nearly 26 GW of new power generation capacity, according to a report from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC). Trump approved a Major Disaster Declaration for North Dakota following a severe storm system that occurred August 7-8, 2025. The storms produced destructive straight-line winds of 70 to 100 mph, large hail, and numerous tornadoes, causing approximately $6 million in damage, primarily to electrical infrastructure. The declaration makes Public Assistance federal funding available through FEMA for emergency work and the repair or replacement of damaged facilities in the counties of Barnes, Grand Forks, Griggs, Kidder, Nelson, Steele, and Stutsman. Funding is also available on a cost-sharing basis for hazard mitigation measures statewide. <4> On October 22, 2025, the investor-led initiative Climate Action 100+ released the sixth round of its Net Zero Company Benchmark assessments. Climate scientists noted that the disaster was severely exacerbated by human-caused global warming, as unseasonably warm temperatures led to heavy rain-on-snow events that rapidly melted the existing snowpack rather than allowing for typical winter snow accumulation. <3> On December 3, 2025, health, environment, and community organizations filed a lawsuit in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit. The lawsuit challenges the EPA's final rule that delayed the implementation of the 2024 methane pollution standards for the oil and gas industry. <4> On December 5, 2025, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) formally proposed a new rule, known as the Safer Affordable Fuel-Efficient (SAFE) Vehicle Rule III, to significantly weaken the Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards. The proposal recalibrates and lowers fuel economy standards for model year 2022 through 2031 passenger cars and light trucks. By no longer factoring in the contribution of electric vehicles to fleet fuel economy, the rule rolls back previous emissions targets finalized under the Biden administration, dropping the estimated 2031 fleetwide requirement from 50.4 miles per gallon (mpg) to 34.5 mpg. The agency estimates this rollback will cut the average up-front vehicle cost associated with CAFE standards by approximately $900. <5> At the UN Climate Change Conference (COP30) in Belém, Brazil, leaders of the U.S. Climate Alliance, including California Governor Gavin Newsom and Wisconsin Governor Tony Evers, reaffirmed state-led commitments to continuing America's climate progress and fighting global warming, particularly in the absence of federal leadership. <6> In August 2025, the U.S. Department of Energy announced nearly $1 billion in funding opportunities aimed at strengthening the domestic critical minerals supply chain. The initiative targets technologies for mining, refining, and manufacturing—materials described as the essential building blocks for electric vehicles, renewable energy storage, and defense technologies. This funding is part of a larger, coordinated North American strategy, involving policy alignment and bilateral alliances with Canada, to aggressively build and support domestic supply chains for the clean energy sector. <7> In the first eight months of 2025, from January through August, the United States added nearly 26 GW of new power generation capacity, according to a report from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC). Solar power was the predominant new energy source during this period, contributing approximately 19 GW, which accounts for about three-quarters of the total new capacity. <8> On October 30, 2025, the U.S. Climate Alliance, America Is All In, and Climate Mayors jointly announced that a delegation of over 100 U.S. local leaders will participate in the 30th U.N. Climate Change Conference (COP30). The conference is scheduled to take place in Belém, Brazil, from November 10 to November 21, 2025. The delegation, led by figures including Wisconsin Governor Tony Evers, New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham, and Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego, aims to demonstrate the United States' sustained subnational climate action and commitment to addressing climate change. <9> On October 23, 2025, President Donald J. Trump approved a Major Disaster Declaration for North Dakota following a severe storm system that occurred August 7-8, 2025. The storms produced destructive straight-line winds of 70 to 100 mph, large hail, and numerous tornadoes, causing approximately $6 million in damage, primarily to electrical infrastructure. The declaration makes Public Assistance federal funding available through FEMA for emergency work and the repair or replacement of damaged facilities in the counties of Barnes, Grand Forks, Griggs, Kidder, Nelson, Steele, and Stutsman. Funding is also available on a cost-sharing basis for hazard mitigation measures statewide.
